nodes.title: Variables and data types
nodes.why: to store and manipulate values in a program
checkpoints: A variable declaration creates a named memory location that can hold a value.
JavaScript primitive types include number, string, boolean, null, undefined, and symbol.
JavaScript variables are dynamically typed, so a variable can later hold a value of a different type; TypeScript instead rejects that assignment at compile time when the declared type differs.
Using const creates a read‑only binding, so the variable cannot be reassigned.

nodes.title: Control flow statements
nodes.why: to direct execution based on conditions and loops
checkpoints: An if statement evaluates a boolean expression and executes the consequent block only when true.
A for loop repeats a block a known number of times, initializing a loop variable, testing a condition, and updating the variable each iteration.
A while loop repeats as long as its condition evaluates to true, checking the condition before each iteration.
Using break exits the nearest enclosing loop, so code after the loop continues execution.

nodes.title: Functions and scope
nodes.why: to encapsulate reusable logic and manage variable visibility
checkpoints: A function definition creates a callable object with its own lexical scope.
Parameters are local variables initialized with the arguments passed at call time.
Variables declared with let or const inside a function are not accessible outside that function.
Returning undefined occurs when a function reaches its end without an explicit return statement.

nodes.title: TypeScript basic types
nodes.why: to add static type information to variables and functions
checkpoints: TypeScript adds type annotations like : number to variable declarations.
When a value's type does not match its annotation, the compiler emits an error.
The any type disables type checking, so any value is assignable to it.
Union types combine multiple possible types using the pipe symbol.

nodes.title: Interfaces and type aliases
nodes.why: to define custom object shapes for compile‑time checking
checkpoints: An interface declares named properties and their types for an object.
A type alias can name any type, including unions and intersections.
An object must have at least the properties required by an interface, otherwise the compiler errors.
Optional properties are marked with ?, so they are omitted without error.

nodes.title: Classes and inheritance
nodes.why: to model objects with behavior and reuse code through extensions
checkpoints: A class defines a constructor and member methods that become part of its prototype.
The extends keyword creates a subclass that inherits members from its parent class.
Super must be called in a subclass constructor before accessing this.
Private fields declared with # are inaccessible outside the class, causing a compile‑time error if accessed.

nodes.title: Generics in TypeScript
nodes.why: to write reusable components that work with multiple types
checkpoints: A generic type parameter is declared in angle brackets after the identifier.
When a generic function is called, the type argument is inferred from the provided arguments.
Specifying a type argument explicitly overrides inference.
Using a generic constraint with extends limits the permitted types.

nodes.title: Modules and imports
nodes.why: to organize code into separate files and manage dependencies
checkpoints: An import statement brings exported bindings from another module into the current scope.
Exported values are declared with export keyword, making them accessible to other modules.
Default export allows a module to expose a single primary value without curly braces.
Circular imports cause runtime undefined values because modules are evaluated sequentially.

nodes.title: Error handling with try/catch
nodes.why: to manage exceptions and keep the program running
checkpoints: A try block executes code that may throw an exception.
When an exception is thrown, control transfers to the matching catch block.
The finally block runs after try or catch, regardless of whether an exception occurred.
Throwing a non‑Error object still triggers catch, but stack traces are missing.

nodes.title: TypeScript configuration
nodes.why: to compile source files with consistent compiler options
checkpoints: The tsconfig.json file defines the root files and compiler options for the project.
Setting target specifies the JavaScript version that the output will conform to.
Strict mode enables a set of type‑checking options that catch common mistakes.
Excluding node_modules prevents the compiler from processing third‑party libraries.
